krum_detection_rate_note: 0.00% in every one of the 25 rounds (25/25) — same as the application-model run. The head-only attack was never detected on this model either.
krum_score_ratio_note: byz_mean_score / honest_mean_score stayed essentially constant at ~0.237 across all 25 rounds (min 0.23693, max 0.23703) — even further below 1.0 than the application model's ~0.38. On this model the Byzantine clients look MORE central relative to the honest spread than they did on application, not less — the blind spot is if anything more pronounced here.

persistent_exclusion_finding.description: The exact same three HONEST clients (1-indexed: 4, 5, 10 — 0-indexed: 3, 4, 9) were discarded by Krum in every single one of the 25 rounds, with no exceptions. Client 4 (1-indexed) in particular scored ~1.24e7 every round — roughly 30x the honest median score — a far larger and more consistent separation than the borderline case this connects to.
persistent_exclusion_finding.connection_to_prior_documented_anomaly: The master doc's Condition 5 section documents a nearly identical, previously-UNRESOLVED anomaly: 'Client 4 (network) persistently excluded 25/25 rounds' under a full-model sign-flip attack with adaptive Krum, hypothesized to be a Dirichlet(alpha=0.7) non-IID sample-distribution skew, not an attack artifact.
persistent_exclusion_finding.implication: This raises a real question about what Krum's bulk-slice scoring is actually responding to in this run: if 3 non-Byzantine clients are excluded every round by a wide margin while the 2 actual Byzantine clients are never flagged, Krum's distance-based decision here appears to be dominated by non-IID structural variance between specific client partitions, not by adversarial deviation at all. This does not change the headline finding (the attack is undetected either way), but it means the 0% detection rate should be read as 'Krum's plaintext-slice scoring is not picking up the attack signal,' not necessarily 'Krum is otherwise working normally and specifically missing this attack' — the mechanism may be more thoroughly broken (by non-IID confounding) than a clean blind-spot story implies.
persistent_exclusion_finding.recommended_follow_up: The master doc's own open item, 'per_client_audit.py proposed but not run against network partitions,' is now more urgent — running it against clients 4, 5, and 10's Dirichlet partitions specifically could confirm or rule out the non-IID skew hypothesis directly.

class_specific_collapse_finding.description: F1 = 0.0000 in every single one of the 25 rounds, without exception — never once produced a usable prediction for this class.
class_specific_collapse_finding.comparison_to_clean_baseline: The master doc's locked clean network baseline (round 22, no attack, no defence) reports Vulnerability_scanner F1 = 0.7198 — a well-learned class under clean conditions. Going from 0.72 to a flat, total 0.0 for the entire run under the undetected head-only attack is a stark, class-specific casualty.
class_specific_collapse_finding.why_this_matters_for_the_writeup: Overall accuracy in this run reaches 90%+ by round 24, which in isolation looks like a healthy, well-trained model. The per-class breakdown shows this is misleading: the majority DDoS classes (UDP, ICMP, TCP) are carrying that aggregate number while Vulnerability_scanner is completely dead. This is a concrete illustration of why an undetected classifier-head attack is dangerous in a way that resists casual detection — a practitioner monitoring only aggregate accuracy would see no red flag at all, while one full attack-relevant class has been silently destroyed.

round_25_instability_finding.description: Best-F1 was reached at round 24 (0.7203), then dropped sharply at round 25 (0.6023), with loss spiking from 4.3704 to 7.5154 in the same step.
round_25_instability_finding.connection_to_prior_pattern: The master doc documents this exact late-round instability pattern recurring 4 independent times already (clean baseline round 25, Condition 5 network round 23, Condition 5 application round 21, Experiment 1's network_dp15 rounds 23->25) and treats it as a structural property of this FedProx/non-IID setup, not noise. This run's round 24->25 drop is consistent with — and arguably a 5th independent occurrence of — that same pattern. Use round 24 (best checkpoint), not round 25 (final), as this run's headline number, per the master doc's existing convention for the network model.

loss_trend_note: Loss does not converge monotonically in this run — it drops through round 11 (0.4401, the run's minimum) then climbs steadily and dramatically to 7.5154 by round 25, even as accuracy and F1-Macro continue to trend upward through round 24. This divergence between loss and accuracy is unusual and consistent with a classifier head being repeatedly corrupted and partially re-corrected each round: the model's discrete predictions (driving accuracy) can stay dominated by a few easy majority classes even while the underlying logits (driving loss) become increasingly poorly calibrated.

comparison_to_application_model_run.both_models_confirm: 0% detection across all 25 rounds, krum_score_ratio well below 1.0 and essentially flat round-to-round, in both models. This is now a cross-model-confirmed finding, not a single-model result.
comparison_to_application_model_run.network_specific_additions: The persistent-exclusion-of-honest-clients anomaly and the total single-class collapse (Vulnerability_scanner) were not present/observed in the application-model run in the same form, and add real texture to the finding beyond just replicating the detection-rate result.

caveats: Single run — no repeat-seed confirmation of the persistent-exclusion or class-collapse findings yet.

The persistent-exclusion finding is a hypothesis connecting to prior documented behavior, not yet independently root-caused — per_client_audit.py (an existing open item in the master doc) has still not been run.
